keep: The idea is named up front: both gauges follow the acid's strength, so both follow the charge, and each is trusted only when rested, corrected, level and mixed.

The float is taught from the floating Dan already has (sinks until it displaces its own weight, rides higher in denser liquid, specific gravity as the relative density he met), so the hydrometer needs no new physics.
One rule in words with a worked number: one point per 1.67 °C from 25 °C, 1.219 at 35 °C corrects to 1.225, and a second case below 25 °C (1.228 at 20 °C to 1.225) in the practice and a mixed puzzle.

Each cited slip has its own DO screen and wrong pick: reading straight after charge (screen 6), the wrong sign on temperature (screens 4 and 11), topping up with acid (screen 8), trusting a layered cell (screen 10).

Every number has a kind: the 1.225 full mark and the 1.105 flat reading are worded as an example cell's, the gauge lines are called sketches, and 2.10 V at about 90 per cent, 4 and 24 hours and the 1.67 °C rule are cited.

The picture follows the brief: hydrometer and voltmeter on the cell, the four traps, the raw reading moving while the corrected one holds, a trust light that waits for all four ticks, and no claim about where a hydrometer samples a layered cell.
fix: Causal step skipped: why layered acid lifts the voltmeter. Add that the lower parts of the plates stand in the strong acid, and stronger acid rests higher, the same rule as before.
False absolute: 'Top up with water, not acid, since only water was lost' is only true of a level that fell by evaporation. Tie it to evaporation in plain words.
Checks that test recall: screen 12 only asks him to recall that 2.10 V is about 90 per cent. Make it a decision across the traps: which of three readings can you trust?
Misconception not shown failing in the explanation: put back what the wrong sign gives (1.213, twelve points short of full) beside the worked correction.
The practice worked example ends on the voltmeter at 2.10 V (about 90 per cent) beside a hydrometer at full, which reads as a contradiction. Drop the voltmeter line from that example.

Paragraph 4 carries the voltmeter, surface charge, layering, the model and the takeaway. Move the level into paragraph 2 with the hydrometer, so paragraph 3 is the voltmeter and paragraph 4 is layering, the model and the recap.
The DO screens give choices but no hints. Give the builder a one-line hint per wrong pick, each naming the slip, so a wrong answer teaches the cause.
The opening's last sentence runs to 23 words. Split it.

shape.ruleInWords: yes: one point per 1.67 °C from 25 °C; rest at least four hours
shape.misconceptionShownFailing: partly: on the puzzles, not in the explanation (fix)
